subject: Chemistry
description: Atomic radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity, metallic character — periodic and group trends

questions.stem: As we go from LEFT to RIGHT across a period, the atomic radius generally:

options.option_text: Decreases (electrons added to same shell, but nuclear charge increases)

questions.explanation: Across a period: same shell, more protons → stronger pull on electrons → smaller radius. Down a group: new shell added → larger radius despite higher Z (effective nuclear charge mitigated by inner-electron screening). So Li > Be > B > C > N > O > F (atomic radii decreasing). Cs is largest naturally-occurring atom. Atomic radius drops from ~152 pm (Li) to ~58 pm (F). Cations smaller than parent atom; anions larger.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The element with the HIGHEST electronegativity is:
questions.explanation: Electronegativity — tendency to attract bonding electrons. Pauling scale (most common): F = 3.98 (highest), O = 3.44, Cl = 3.16, N = 3.04. Top right of periodic table = highest electronegativity (excluding noble gases which don't normally form bonds). Bottom left = lowest (Cs, Fr ~0.7). Difference in electronegativity > 1.7 → ionic bond; < 0.4 → non-polar covalent; in between → polar covalent. Electronegativity drives polarity (water is polar — H-O), reactivity, hydrogen-bonding.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Ionisation energy (the energy to remove an outer electron) generally:

options.option_text: Decreases left to right across a period
Increases left to right across a period; decreases down a group

questions.explanation: IE trends OPPOSITE to atomic radius. Across a period: nuclear charge ↑ → outer electron held tighter → IE ↑. Down a group: shells ↑ → outer electron farther away → easier to remove → IE ↓. He has highest first IE (2,372 kJ/mol). Cs has lowest. Exceptions — Be > B (2s² stability), N > O (half-filled 2p³ stability of N). Ionisation values are a fingerprint of orbital structure — anomalies reveal half-filled and fully-filled subshell stability.
questions.subject: Chemistry

options.option_text: Increases left to right across a period
Decreases left to right across a period; increases down a group

questions.explanation: Metallic character — willingness to lose electrons. Highest at bottom-left (Cs, Fr); lowest at top-right (F, He). Across a period: tendency to lose decreases (atoms get more electronegative). Down a group: outer electrons farther from nucleus → easily lost → more metallic. Diagonal stairstep separates metals (left) from non-metals (right); metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit on the staircase. Most reactive metal — Fr (or Cs); most reactive non-metal — F.

questions.stem: The modern periodic table has elements arranged in order of increasing:
questions.explanation: Modern Periodic Law (Henry Moseley, 1913): Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number (Z). Resolved anomalies in Mendeleev's mass-based table — e.g., Ar (Z=18, mass 40) vs K (Z=19, mass 39) — Mendeleev's order had to swap them; Moseley's law put them right. The modern table has 118 confirmed elements (last addition: Oganesson Z=118, named 2016). 7 periods, 18 groups (in extended form). Lanthanides + actinides shown as f-block at bottom for compactness.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The two groups in the periodic table containing elements that are gases at room temperature are:

options.option_text: Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 2 (alkaline earth metals)

questions.explanation: Halogens (Group 17): F₂, Cl₂ are gases (Br₂ is a liquid; I₂, At — solids). Noble gases (Group 18): all 6 are gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). Plus H (Group 1 by some, group 17 by others) is a gas. N₂, O₂ are also gases (Groups 15, 16). Most metals are solids; mercury (Hg, Group 12) is liquid; Cs, Ga, Br near room-temperature melting (Cs melts ~28 °C). Most elements are solids at STP.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The longest period in the modern periodic table contains:
questions.explanation: Period 6 — 32 elements when lanthanides counted in (Cs Z=55 to Rn Z=86, with La 57 + 14 lanthanides + Hf 72 onwards). Same for Period 7 (32, with actinides). Period 1 — only 2 (H, He). Periods 2 & 3 — 8 each (s + p). Periods 4 & 5 — 18 each (s + d + p). Period 6 = 2 (s) + 14 (f, lanthanides) + 10 (d) + 6 (p) = 32. Some standard table layouts split the f-block out for visual compactness.
